To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of death in patients with RENAL ARTERY STENOSIS is determined by clinical, in addition anatomic and physiological factors.
patients with renal artery stenoses have an elevated risk of death and that the risk factors for mortality include left ventricular dysfunction and a history of prior MI.
patients with renal artery stenoses and 2 or 1 mortality risks factors, respectively, have a 2-fold and 1.5-fold higher risk of death than patients without these risk factors.

atherosclerotic renovascular disease, a disease that is common, yet under-recognized and under-treated.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients with a low LVEF and previous MI are at higher risk of dying and that these patients should be excluded from future renal artery stenting trials.

patients with atherosclerotic RAS have a high mortality rate, but renal artery stenting improves survival in patients without previous MI or LVEF ≤ 35%, and in patients with 1 of these 2 risk factors, but not in patients with both.

The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with a low LVEF and/or a previous MI are at higher risk of mortality and that renal artery stenting in these patients does not improve survival.

patients with renal artery stenoses who also have a history of myocardial infarctions or left ventricular ejections fraction of 35% or less have worse survival than patients with renal artery disease alone.
